chunks: "I start from the system requirements, not the datasheet. What does it have to sense, drive and talk to, how fast, on what power, in what environment, and at what cost?
Then I translate that into numbers. CPU: I take the fastest loop and count cycles.
For a 20 kilohertz motor-control loop on a 72 megahertz core I have 3,600 cycles per iteration, and I'd want the algorithm under about half of that for headroom.
Does it need a floating-point unit or DSP instructions?.
Memory: estimate flash for code plus bootloader and any update image, and RAM for buffers and stacks, then add 30 to 50 percent margin.
Peripherals: count what I need and check the pins can actually be routed: timers with the right outputs, ADC channels and sample rate, UART, SPI, I2C, CAN or USB, DMA channels.
A feature on the datasheet isn't usable if it's muxed onto a pin I've used.
Power: the supply range, active current per MHz, and sleep current for a battery product, plus wake-up time and what stays alive in sleep.

Then the practical ones: operating temperature range and qualification, package and pin count, debug support, toolchain and library support, errata, cost at volume, and availability, ideally with a pin-compatible family so I can scale flash up or down without a respin.
And I'd keep the choice flexible by designing in a family, not a single part."
